rows.source: HSE metalworking-fluid health-risk guidance
rows.verified: Metalworking fluids are neat oils or water-based fluids used to lubricate and cool metal machining and shaping operations.

rows.source: HSE metalworking-fluid health-risk guidance
rows.verified: Exposure to metalworking fluids can cause dermatitis and respiratory diseases including occupational asthma and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

rows.source: HSE metalworking-fluid health-risk guidance
rows.verified: Exposure can occur by inhaling mist, direct skin contact, entry through broken skin or ingestion associated with poor hygiene.

rows.source: HSE metalworking-fluid health-risk guidance
rows.verified: COSHH requires metalworking-fluid exposure to be prevented where reasonably practicable or otherwise adequately controlled.

rows.source: HSE metalworking-fluid health-risk guidance
rows.verified: Fluid quality and bacterial contamination should be maintained and controlled while skin exposure and airborne mist are minimised.

rows.source: HSE metalworking-fluid health-risk guidance
rows.verified: Enclosures and local exhaust ventilation used as exposure controls must be checked and maintained.

rows.source: HSE metalworking-fluid health-risk guidance
rows.verified: Water-mix systems should normally be checked for bacterial contamination with dipslides once a week unless effective fluid-quality management justifies a lower frequency.

rows.source: HSE metalworking-fluid health-risk guidance
rows.verified: Where fluid or mist exposure cannot be prevented, health surveillance should include appropriate skin and respiratory checks with occupational-health escalation for positive findings.

rows.source: HSE metalworking-fluid health-risk guidance
rows.verified: Metalworking-fluid risk depends on fluid chemistry, mist generation, bacterial condition, concentration, pH, enclosure, LEV, skin contact and surveillance findings.

rows.source: HSE metalworking-fluid health-risk guidance
rows.verified: General mist, skin exposure, bacterial contamination, control maintenance and health surveillance guidance does not prove the current condition, exposure or control performance at an individual parcel and does not establish an exact event or illness probability.

rows.source: HSE occupational dermatitis and skin-exposure guidance
rows.verified: Dermatitis can be caused by skin contact with irritants or by an allergic reaction to a sensitising substance.

rows.source: HSE occupational dermatitis and skin-exposure guidance
rows.verified: Signs can include redness, scaling, blistering, weeping, cracking and swelling, with symptoms such as itching and pain.

rows.source: HSE occupational dermatitis and skin-exposure guidance
rows.verified: Repeated wet work, including more than about 20 hand washes or wet hands for more than two hours in a shift, can cause irritant dermatitis.

rows.source: HSE occupational dermatitis and skin-exposure guidance
rows.verified: Common irritants include soaps, detergents, solvents, oils, greases, dusts, acids, alkalis and wet cement.

rows.source: HSE occupational dermatitis and skin-exposure guidance
rows.verified: Once a person becomes sensitised to an allergen, the sensitisation is likely to be permanent and renewed contact can trigger allergic dermatitis.

rows.source: HSE occupational dermatitis and skin-exposure guidance
rows.verified: Employers must assess dermatitis risks and provide adequate controls, information, instruction and training where a risk exists.

rows.source: HSE occupational dermatitis and skin-exposure guidance
rows.verified: Prevention includes avoiding contact where possible, protecting skin appropriately and using moisturisers to replenish natural oils.

rows.source: HSE occupational dermatitis and skin-exposure guidance
rows.verified: Workers should check their skin regularly and report early itching, dryness or redness because early treatment is more effective.

rows.source: HSE occupational dermatitis and skin-exposure guidance
rows.verified: Dermatitis risk depends on substance, wet-work duration, concentration, contact route, glove choice, hygiene, individual sensitisation and early health-surveillance findings.

rows.source: HSE occupational dermatitis and skin-exposure guidance
rows.verified: General recognition, prevention and control of irritant and allergic occupational skin disease guidance does not prove the current condition, exposure or control performance at an individual parcel and does not establish an exact event or illness probability.
